summary: At barely 0.9 square miles, Citrus is one of the most densely packed census-designated places in the San Gabriel Valley — over 12,000 people per square mile crammed into a footprint smaller than many regional parks — yet it sits against the dramatic backdrop of the San Gabriel Mountains, whose snow-dusted winter peaks are visible from ordinary residential streets. That geographic contrast defines the place: an intensely built-out grid of homes and strip-commercial stretches with almost no breathing room, yet framed by some of Southern California's most impressive vertical terrain. The median home value of $614,200 against a median household income of about $101,000 yields a price-to-income ratio near 6:1, which means purchasing requires substantial savings or dual-income math even at above-average earnings; rents averaging $2,204 consume roughly 26 percent of that median gross income, landing just inside conventional affordability thresholds. Citrus functions almost entirely as a bedroom community — the San Gabriel Valley's job centers in healthcare, logistics, and education are a freeway commute away along the I-210 or I-10 corridors, and switching employers rarely means staying local. With 9.3 hours of daily sunshine and average highs around 77°F, the climate is classically interior Southern California — warm, dry, and reliably bright, though summer heat in the valley floor pushes well past comfortable without air conditioning. The essential tension here is proximity without autonomy: mountain views and freeway access to greater Los Angeles, but almost no local employment base or distinct commercial identity to anchor daily life within the community itself.
